5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3 items are needed for a steady-state 13C metabolic flux analysis.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is essential to set up the atom transitions and the mass balance constraints that define the network topology and the mapping of carbon atoms through the reactions.

6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the fluxes; the measured mass isotopomer distributions are fitted to the labeling simulations.

3. Biomass composition of the organism is also required to close the network. The biomass drain must be defined in terms of protein, lipids, carbohydrates etc. so that carbon and redox balances can be written and the system of flux equations is fully determined at steady state.

Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not needed for the classic steady-state 13C-MFA formulation. Cell density is a cultivation parameter, and kinetics and regulation are not used once the network is at isotopic and metabolic steady state.

3.text:
In a textbook steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained from a
stoichiometric isotopomer balance

    S . v = 0
    M(v) . x = 0

where S is the network stoichiometric matrix, v the flux vector and x the
vector of isotopomer / mass isotopologue fractions. 

Hence the formal inputs to the isotopomer balance are

* the carbon atom transition network, i.e. the reaction stoichiometry and
the mapping of carbon atoms through the network. Item 1 is therefore
essential. In practice the network has to be closed with a biomass drain.
The biomass drain is written as a formal reaction

    Σ c_i M_i → Biomass

whose stoichiometric coefficients c_i are obtained from the measured
biomass composition, protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc., and the growth rate.
That is the usual way the biomass sink is introduced into S for a
complete 13C-MFA and it is why the biomass composition is always used in
the practical implementation. 

* the experimental data that constrain the isotopomer balances. That is the
measured mass isotopologue / 13C enrichment pattern of intracellular
metabolic intermediates, Item 6, together with the measured extracellular
exchange fluxes which are normally expressed per unit biomass. The
measured labelling pattern is the 13C-MFA specific input which distinguishes
it from ordinary stoichiometric flux balance analysis.

Enzyme kinetics, the regulatory wiring of the network and the absolute
maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor are not used in the
steady-state isotopomer balance. Steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric
and isotopic constraint problem and is completely parameter-free with
respect to kinetics and regulation.

In the minimal formal sense the two independent experimental inputs are
therefore the stoichiometric network, 1, and the intracellular 13C labelling
patterns, 6. With the conventional closure of the network the biomass
reaction is written explicitly with the measured biomass composition, item
3, so that in practice the three items 1,3 and 6 are used and items 2,4 and
5 – maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks – are not
required for a steady state 13C-MFA. If biomass composition is regarded as
part of the definition of the stoichiometric biomass reaction, the two
distinct experimental requirements are stoichiometry and isotopic labelling.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would say 3 of the listed items are needed for a steady-state 13C-MFA.

Stoichiometry is essential to write the mass balance equations and define the atom transitions for each reaction. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the fluxes via isotopomer balancing. Biomass composition is also required in practice because the biomass drain has to be explicitly defined in the network with a proper biomass reaction. The measured fractions of protein, lipid and carbohydrate set the carbon demand and the elemental formula of the biomass sink, so the system is closed and the flux distribution is uniquely identifiable. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used in the classical steady-state 13C-MFA formulation; steady state is an assumption on pools, not a kinetic or regulatory model.

1.text:
In a strictly isotopomer based steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained
from the coupling of a stoichiometric network with the measured 13C
atom transition patterns.  

* Atom balances give for every reaction i

    v i S i = 0

with S the stoichiometric matrix of the network which is defined by 1.
Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. The network can be written without any
kinetic or regulatory information.

* The 13C information is introduced through the isotopomer balances

    v · f = 0

where f is the vector of fractional labelling, i.e. the measured
mass isotopomer or NMR multiplet distributions of the intracellular
metabolites, 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates.
The labeling data are the experimental constraints that make the
underdetermined stoichiometric system identifiable. Once the network and the
labeling data are known the steady state internal fluxes v can be obtained
by non-linear fitting of the simulated labeling to the measured labeling.

Enzyme kinetics 4. and the regulatory network 5. are not used in a
steady state flux balance / isotopomer balance formulation and the
maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor 2. is a scale up / process
parameter and plays no role in the flux calculation.

In practice a closed whole cell model is normally written with an explicit
biomass formation reaction. To write that reaction one needs the
elemental / macromolecular biomass composition 3. Biomass composition of
the organism, i.e. the protein/lipid/carbohydrate carbon demand which
together with the measured growth rate defines the biomass sink and closes
the carbon balance. With that closure the operational set of data that is
usually quoted for a 13C-MFA is 1 + 3 + 6, stoichiometry + a defined
biomass reaction + measured 13C labeling. The strictly isotopomer
mathematical requirement is the stoichiometric network and the measured
13C labeling, 1 and 6, i.e. two of the six listed items, with the biomass
composition being the conventional practical closure.

7.text:
In a strictly isotopic sense steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric/isotope
mapping problem. Fluxes are obtained by fitting the network fluxes to the
measured isotopomer / mass isotopomer distributions under the steady state
constraints

dCi/dt = 0   and   dMi/dt = 0

where Ci is the concentration of metabolite i and Mi is its labelling
state. 

* Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with atom transitions is indispensable.
The network defines the mass balance constraints

S . v = 0

and the atom mapping that maps the labelling state of precursors onto
products, i.e. the labelling model Mi(v). Without a stoichiometric network
with defined atom transitions no isotopomer simulation can be made.

* Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is the experimental
data that the fluxes are fitted to. At isotopic steady state the measured
mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular, and usually also extracellular,
metabolites, e.g. MID from MS/NMR of a 13C tracer experiment, provide the
data vector which is matched to the simulation Mi(v). No kinetic
information is used in the fit.

That is the mathematical core of 13C-MFA. Enzyme kinetics and regulatory
networks are not required, and the maximum cell density of the organism in
a bioreactor is irrelevant for the isotopic fit. 

In practice the network is closed with an explicit biomass drain. The
biomass drain reaction is normally written from a measured or literature
biomass composition, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipids, carbohydrates
etc., together with a measured specific growth rate μ, so that the carbon
lost to biomass can be accounted for in the carbon balance and the
precursor fluxes to amino acids, nucleotides etc. can be expressed. With
that conventional closure the three routinely used inputs are

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry + atom mapping
3. Biomass composition to define the biomass reaction / carbon balance
6. Measured 13C labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates

Extracellular fluxes, including biomass formation rate, are also measured
in practice. If biomass is treated as a lumped, unlabelled sink the
biomass composition can be formally kept out of the isotopic fit and the
strictly indispensable inputs for the isotopic calculation are 1 and 6,
i.e. two of the six items listed, the stoichiometry and the labelling data.
Enzyme kinetics, regulatory networks and maximum cell density are not used
in steady state 13C-MFA.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3. For isotopic steady state 13C-MFA you need the atom-mapped network to set up the mass and isotopic balances, i.e. metabolic reaction stoichiometry, and you need the experimental constraints that come from the 13C labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates to resolve flux reversals and cycle splitting. The third essential piece in practice is a properly defined biomass sink. Biomass composition, the fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., is required to formulate the biomass formation reaction stoichiometry and to close carbon and redox balances at steady state. That is the conventional way to get a closed metabolic model for flux estimation. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are bioprocess/kinetic/control information and are not used in the stoichiometric/isotope mapping formulation of steady-state 13C-MFA.

11.text:
13C-MFA at metabolic steady state is a stoichiometric / isotopomer problem, not a kinetic / regulatory one.

The flux solution is obtained from the stoichiometric network together with the
measured carbon atom transitions in the network. In practice that is

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. The network has to be written as a
set of mass balanced reactions so that the usual S . v =0 steady state
constraints and the atom mapping / isotopomer balances can be written down.
The biomass formation reaction is part of that stoichiometric description.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. The mass
isotopomer distributions, MIDs, measured by MS/NMR for intracellular
metabolites are the experimental constraints that resolve the otherwise
underdetermined flux degrees of freedom of the stoichiometric model.

In a closed, growth-coupled implementation the biomass sink has to be
defined. That is normally done with the measured biomass composition,
3. Biomass composition of the organism, i.e. the fraction of protein,
lipid, carbohydrate etc. which fixes the stoichiometric coefficients of
the biomass reaction. Once the biomass reaction is in the stoichiometric
model the composition is in fact already contained in 1.

The items which are not needed for steady state 13C-MFA are

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. Absolute
rates are normally expressed per gram dry weight or per cell, the maximum
attainable density is irrelevant for the flux ratios that 13C-MFA resolves.
The actual steady state growth rate / extracellular exchange rates are
needed, not the maximum cell density.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks. 13C-MFA is a
constraint-based, non-kinetic method. Kinetic parameters and regulatory
information are not used to obtain the steady state flux distribution.

In the minimal list from the six items the strictly essential information
is 1 and 6, i.e. stoichiometry + measured 13C labelling. This is normally
taught as the practical three item set 1,3,6 – stoichiometry, a defined
biomass composition/biomass reaction and the intracellular 13C labelling
patterns – with 2,4 and 5 being unnecessary for steady state 13C-MFA.

17.text:
In a 13C steady state MFA the fluxes are obtained from the fit of a
stoichiometric / atom-mapping model to measured isotopomer data under
the assumption of metabolic and isotopic steady state.  That is
different from kinetic or regulatory modelling.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is indispensable.  The atom
transition matrix that defines how carbon atoms are mapped from
substrates to products in every reaction in the network is the
skeleton on which the isotopomer balancing equations are built.  In
practice the network is closed with a biomass drain reaction and the
biomass drain is written with the usual biomass composition, i.e.
fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., so that the carbon
demand for growth is accounted for in the stoichiometric model.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the
experimental data that the model is fitted to.  Measured mass
isotopomer distributions, e.g. MIDs from MS or NMR, for intracellular
intermediates together with the measured extracellular fluxes provide
the constraints that make the flux distribution identifiable.

These are the core MFA inputs.  The three items that are not needed
for a 13C steady state MFA are

* 2. Maximum cell density in a bioreactor.  Cell density is a process
parameter. MFA works with specific rates, i.e. per biomass or per
volume, at isotopic steady state, not with the attainable maximum
density.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics. Kinetic parameters are required for kinetic
flux modelling or for dynamic MFA, not for the stoichiometric/
isotopomer steady state formulation.
* 5. Regulatory networks.  Regulatory information is not used in the
stoichiometric isotopomer balancing.

Hence in the strict isotopomer fitting sense the indispensable
information from the list is the network stoichiometry and the
intracellular labelling data, items 1 and 6.  In routine practice the
stoichiometric model is made operational by writing a biomass
formation reaction with the organism specific biomass composition,
item 3, so that the network is mass balanced and the flux to biomass
can be quantified.  With that practical closure the three items
commonly quoted are 1, 3 and 6, whereas 2, 4 and 5 are not required
for steady state 13C MFA.

15.text:
In a strictly stoichiometric 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained from
the atom balance equations

    S . v = 0
    M(v) = m_exp

together with the measured mass isotopomer distributions. 

* S is the stoichiometric matrix of the network that is used for the
atom-transition mappings. Without a defined stoichiometry and atom map
the relation between a flux distribution and the labelling that it
produces cannot be written down, so 1. metabolic reaction stoichiometry
is an absolute requirement.

* The labelling equations are closed by the experimental mass isotopomer
distributions of the intracellular intermediates that are measured by
MS/NMR. The 13C-MFA problem is the problem of finding a v which
reproduces the measured MIDs. Hence 6. the isotope labelling patterns
of metabolic intermediates is the second absolute requirement.

Enzyme kinetics 4., regulatory information 5. and the bioreactor
operational parameter maximum cell density 2. are not used in a
steady-state stoichiometric flux analysis. The flux calculation is
thermodynamic/ stoichiometric, not kinetic, and it is carried out at
metabolic steady state, dC/dt = 0, i.e. at constant pool sizes and
constant labelling, so that maximal growth / maximal cell density is
irrelevant.

In any closed implementation the network has to be closed to a biomass
sink. The biomass sink is normally written as a linear combination of
precursor metabolites whose stoichiometric coefficients are obtained from
the measured or literature biomass composition, i.e. the protein/lipid/
carbohydrate – and hence amino acid/nucleotide/fatty acid – demand of
the organism. In practice 3. biomass composition is therefore used to
define the biomass drain reaction that closes the carbon balance and
allows absolute flux normalisation.  If the biomass reaction is taken as
a given black-box sink the strictly mathematical requirements of the
13C labelling equations are 1 and 6, i.e. two of the six items listed,
stoichiometry + labelling.  This is the three-item experimental
implementation 1, 3 and 6 that is normally quoted in the literature, the
stoichiometry, the biomass composition needed for the biomass drain and
the measured 13C labelling patterns, with 2, 4 and 5 being unnecessary
for steady-state 13C-MFA.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3 items are required. 

For a steady-state 13C-MFA you need a defined stoichiometric network, 1, to write the mass balance and atom-mapping constraints. You also need the measured isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, 6, because those patterns are what constrain the flux split ratios via the isotopomer balances. In practice the biomass formation reaction has to be defined in the stoichiometric model, which requires the biomass composition, 3, i.e. the fractional protein, lipid and carbohydrate makeup, to close the carbon and redox balances at steady state. 

Maximum cell density, 2, is a bioprocess scale parameter and enzyme kinetics, 4, and regulatory networks, 5, are not used in the steady-state isotopomer balance formulation, so they are not required for the core 13C-MFA.

6.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux vector v is obtained from the
steady state mass balances

    S . v = 0

together with the 13C labelling constraints.  In practice the
problem is

        min v   ||  xsim(v, S) – xmeas ||

subject to S v = 0 and v ≥ 0, where xsim is the labelling pattern
predicted from the network by the cumomer / isotopomer balances and
xmeas is the measured labelling.

Hence the two pieces of information that are mathematically
unavoidable are

* 1. The metabolic reaction stoichiometry S.  The stoichiometric
matrix is needed for the steady-state mass balance constraints and
for the propagation of 13C label through the network.  Without a
stoichiometric network there is no S v = 0 and no isotopomer
balance to solve.

* 6. The experimentally measured isotope labelling patterns of
metabolic intermediates, most conveniently the proteinogenic amino
acids or intracellular free metabolites derived from them.  The
labelling data are the constraints that make the flux split
uniquely identifiable.  In the limit S v = 0 alone 13C-MFA is
under-determined.

Maximum cell density in the bioreactor, enzyme kinetic parameters
and regulatory network topology are not used in the steady state
isotopomer balance formulation.  Steady state extracellular specific
rates, growth rate etc. are required experimentally but they are not
listed here.

In routine practice the biomass drain is written as a pseudo-reaction

    Biomass = Σ c i Pi

with c i the fractional composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate
etc.  The biomass composition 3 is therefore normally used to close
the stoichiometric network and to convert a measured growth rate into
a carbon drain from central metabolism.  With that operational
convention the model that is actually solved uses 1, 3 and 6, i.e.
stoichiometry + biomass definition + measured 13C labelling, while
2, 4 and 5 remain unnecessary for a steady state 13C-MFA.  The two
mathematically essential items are 1 and 6.

4.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are estimated from the
stoichiometric constraints of the network together with the constraints
that the measured isotopic distributions impose on the atom transitions.

* S v = 0   is the steady state mass balance.
The atom transition network, i.e. the metabolic reaction stoichiometry
in the sense of the carbon atom mappings, is therefore indispensable.
It is the stoichiometric matrix S, including the biomass drain reaction,
on which the flux variables are defined. Without a defined network the
isotopic constraints cannot be written down.

* The isotopic constraints themselves. The flux dependent steady state
isotopomer balances are

      v·E = 0

where E is the set of expected labelling patterns for the
intermediates. Those expected patterns are obtained from the measured
13C labelling of intracellular metabolites, or in practice of their
proteinogenic proxies, i.e. the measured isotope labelling patterns of
metabolic intermediates / amino acids. That is the experimental
information that makes the flux estimation uniquely solvable beyond
simple stoichiometric balancing.

That is the core of a 13C-MFA. Enzyme kinetics 4, regulatory networks 5
and the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor 2 are not used
in a stoichiometric, steady state 13C-MFA.

In practice the network is normally closed with a biomass formation
reaction. The stoichiometric coefficients of that drain reaction are
obtained from the measured biomass composition, i.e. the fractional
protein, lipid and carbohydrate content and the growth rate, which is
why the biomass composition 3 is routinely quoted as a third practical
input for a closed, carbon balanced 13C-MFA model. Strictly speaking the
core mathematical requirement is stoichiometry + labelling, i.e. items 1
and 6, two inputs, which becomes the commonly quoted three inputs 1,
3 and 6 when the biomass sink is written explicitly.

12.text:
In steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the mass and
isotopomer balance of the network

v . S = 0
and

M(v , x) = m meas

where S is the stoichiometric matrix of the network, v the vector of
unknown fluxes and m meas the measured mass isotopomer distributions of
the intracellular metabolites, generally obtained from proteinogenic
amino acids. The problem is therefore a stoichiometric + isotopomer
inverse problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Required. The stoichiometric
matrix S and the atom mapping that defines how carbon atoms are
transferred in each reaction are the basis of both the mass balance
v . S = 0 and of the isotopomer balance equations. Without a defined
network and an atom map no 13C fluxes can be calculated.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Required.
The measured 13C labeling of intracellular - or in practice
extracellular/proteinogenic - metabolites provides the experimental
constraints m meas that make the flux solution identifiable. In the
steady state formulation it is the 13C distribution that breaks the
flux balance degeneracy of S alone.

The remaining items are not part of a conventional steady state
13C-MFA.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. Not
required. Cell density / biomass concentration is a scale factor for
absolute rates. Steady state 13C-MFA works with specific rates,
e.g. mmol gDW-1 h-1, and with the measured specific uptake/secretion
and growth rates. A maximum achievable density is a bioprocess
limitation and is irrelevant for the isotopomer flux estimation.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. Not required. Kinetic constants, Vmax, Km,
etc., are needed for kinetic modelling and for dynamic MFA. Steady
state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric/inotopomer constrained optimisation/
fitting problem and is formally independent of enzyme kinetics and of
regulation.

* 5. Regulatory networks. Not required. Regulatory information is
not used in the isotopomer balance equations. Regulation may explain
why a flux is what it is, it does not enter the calculation of the flux
from stoichiometry and labelling.

* 3. Biomass composition. Not a strictly independent requirement for
the isotopomer calculation itself. The biomass formation can be entered
as a measured sink flux v biomass = µ, the specific growth rate, together
with the stoichiometric biomass drain reaction that is already part of
the network stoichiometry in item 1. In practice the biomass reaction
is formulated from the macromolecular composition - protein, lipid,
carbohydrate, etc. - so that item 3 is the practical way to build the
biomass stoichiometry that is contained in S. If the biomass reaction
is taken as given in the stoichiometric network, no separate
composition data are needed for the 13C flux solve, the core
information is items 1 and 6. If the formulation of the biomass reaction
is counted as a separate prerequisite the commonly quoted practical
set is stoichiometry + biomass composition + labelling data, i.e. items
1, 3 and 6.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3

For a steady-state 13C-MFA you need a defined atom-mapped stoichiometric network to set up the mass-balance and atom transitions, 1, and you need the measured 13C labeling patterns of the intracellular intermediates to constrain the fluxes, 6. A third definitional requirement is the biomass composition. The biomass formation reaction has to be included in the stoichiometric model to close the system at steady state, and its stoichiometry is defined from the measured fractions of protein, lipids and carbohydrates etc. 3. That defines the drain for the precursors and allows calculation of the biomass flux from the extracellular rates. Maximum cell density, 2, enzyme kinetics, 4, and regulatory networks, 5, are not used in the steady-state 13C isotopomer analysis itself. So the practical minimal set is stoichiometry, biomass composition and labeling data.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would say 3 pieces of information are needed.

Steady-state 13C-MFA is built on a stoichiometric network, so metabolic reaction stoichiometry is essential to write the mass balance and atom-mapping constraints. The isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that actually constrain the flux solution, without them you have no 13C information to fit. You also need the biomass composition, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, to define a proper biomass drain reaction and close the carbon and redox balances in the model; otherwise the fluxes into biomass cannot be accounted for and the system is underdetermined. 

Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not required for a stoichiometric, steady-state 13C-MFA – kinetics and regulation inform dynamic behaviour but not the flux solution under the steady-state assumption, and cell density is a bioprocess scale parameter, not a flux constraint. So stoichiometry, biomass composition and measured labeling patterns are the minimal set.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For a steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained from
stoichiometry + isotopic mass balance, not from kinetics or regulation.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry – required. The atom transition 
network that maps carbon atoms from one metabolite to another is the
skeleton on which the isotopomer balances are written. No flux can be
identified without a defined network topology and atom mapping.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates – required.
The measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. from MS/NMR of proteinogenic amino acids or intracellular intermediates, are the experimental data that constrain the flux split ratios in the network. In the isotopic steady state

dM/dt = 0  ⇔  S·v =0  and  T(v)·M =0

the second balance is the 13C labelling balance and is supplied by the
experimental MID data.

The other three items are not part of a 13C-MFA per se.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – irrelevant for 
flux identification. Cell density / titre is a bioprocess scale-up parameter
and does not enter the stoichiometric/isotopomer balances.

4. Enzyme kinetics – not required. Steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric
analysis. Vmax, Km, regulation etc. are not used to compute the flux
distribution, they are only needed for kinetic or dynamic MFA.

5. Regulatory networks – not required. The flux distribution is inferred
from the isotopic data under the assumption of metabolic and isotopic
steady state; regulatory information is not used in the calculation.

3. Biomass composition – is not a strict input for the isotopic
calculation itself. The isotopic balances are closed by measured
extracellular uptake/secretion rates and the measured MIDs.
In practice a biomass drain reaction is written for the network and the
drain stoichiometry is normally obtained from a measured biomass
composition / elemental formula and a measured growth rate, so
biomass composition is routinely used in the conventional implementation
of a complete steady state 13C-MFA. If the biomass reaction is taken as a
given part of the network stoichiometry, the core strictly required
information from the list is 1 + 6, i.e. two items, and in the usual
laboratory workflow the biomass composition is the third routinely supplied
item, 1 + 3 + 6.

18.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are inferred from the way 13C is
distributed through a known chemical network. The inference is therefore
a purely stoichiometric / isotopomer balance problem and it is
kinetically and regulatory independent.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry  –  required. 
The network that is used for the flux estimation has to be defined in
terms of reactions and, for 13C, atom mappings. The stoichiometric matrix
S and the carbon atom transition maps are the structure on which the
mass balance S v = 0 and the isotopomer balance equations are built.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates – required.
The measurable data that constrain the flux vector v are the
experimentally determined mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. the
13C fractions of proteinogenic amino acids, intracellular organic acids
etc., obtained by MS/NMR after feeding a labelled substrate. The
simulation of the labelling pattern from a candidate flux distribution
is compared with the measured pattern and the fluxes are optimised to
minimise the mismatch. No labelling data, no 13C-MFA.

Items 4 and 5 are not used. 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric flux
identifiability problem at isotopic steady state, enzyme kinetics and
regulatory information are not part of the model.

Item 2, the maximal cell density reached in a bioreactor, is not a
parameter of the isotopic steady state flux problem. Specific
extracellular rates are needed at the steady state of interest, not the
maximal attainable density.

In routine practice the network is closed with a biomass formation
reaction. The stoichiometric coefficients of that reaction are obtained
from the elemental/ macromolecular composition of the biomass, i.e. the
fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., that is item 3. Once the
biomass equation is defined it is in practice part of the stoichiometric
model 1. If the biomass equation is taken as already contained in the
stoichiometric model the strictly indispensable experimental data for a
steady state 13C-MFA are therefore the network stoichiometry/atom map
and the measured intracellular labelling pattern. With the conventional
closure of the network with a defined biomass reaction the three items
1, 3 and 6 are the ones that are normally used, and 2, 4 and 5 are not
required for the 13C-MFA per se.  This is usually quoted as the two
core requirements, stoichiometry + labelling, i.e. 1 and 6, and
three practical requirements 1, 3 and 6.

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the strict 13C-MFA formalism the flux solution is obtained from
stoichiometry + isotopomer balance at metabolic steady state.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry – Yes. The stoichiometric matrix S
v=0 at steady state and the atom-mapping that defines how 13C atoms are
transferred from one metabolite to the next is the structural constraint
that couples fluxes to labelling.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates – Yes. The
measured mass isotopomer distributions of proteinogenic amino acids,
intracellular pools etc. obtained after feeding a 13C tracer provide the
experimental constraints that make the under-determined stoichiometric
system identifiable. Extracellular uptake / secretion rates are the
additional experimental data that are normally supplied with the
labelling.

The other three items are not needed for the 13C-MFA calculation per se.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – No. Cell
density is a scale factor. What is used is the specific uptake/secretion
and growth rates normalised to biomass, not the maximal attainable
density.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics – No. 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric / isotopomer
analysis. No kinetic parameters or Vmax, Km etc. are used in the steady
state balance.

* 5. Regulatory networks – No. Regulation is not part of the steady state
mass and carbon atom balance.

That is the minimal, strictly indispensable set, 1 and 6, i.e. 2 of the
six items. In practice the network is normally closed with a biomass
drain reaction. To write that drain in a chemically meaningful way the
macromolecular composition of the biomass, 3. Biomass composition of the
organism i.e. fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, is then
supplied together with the measured growth rate so that the flux to
biomass is known. With that conventional closure the working set is
1,3 and 6, three items, the stoichiometry, the biomass definition and
the measured 13C labelling. Enzyme kinetics, regulatory information and
maximum bioreactor cell density remain unnecessary for the 13C steady
state flux calculation.

public_text.5:
3 items are needed for a steady-state 13C metabolic flux analysis.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is essential to set up the atom transitions and the mass balance constraints that define the network topology and the mapping of carbon atoms through the reactions.

6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the fluxes; the measured mass isotopomer distributions are fitted to the labeling simulations.

3. Biomass composition of the organism is also required to close the network. The biomass drain must be defined in terms of protein, lipids, carbohydrates etc. so that carbon and redox balances can be written and the system of flux equations is fully determined at steady state.

Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not needed for the classic steady-state 13C-MFA formulation. Cell density is a cultivation parameter, and kinetics and regulation are not used once the network is at isotopic and metabolic steady state.

In a textbook steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained from a
stoichiometric isotopomer balance

    S . v = 0
    M(v) . x = 0

where S is the network stoichiometric matrix, v the flux vector and x the
vector of isotopomer / mass isotopologue fractions. 

Hence the formal inputs to the isotopomer balance are

* the carbon atom transition network, i.e. the reaction stoichiometry and
the mapping of carbon atoms through the network. Item 1 is therefore
essential. In practice the network has to be closed with a biomass drain.
The biomass drain is written as a formal reaction

    Σ c_i M_i → Biomass

whose stoichiometric coefficients c_i are obtained from the measured
biomass composition, protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc., and the growth rate.
That is the usual way the biomass sink is introduced into S for a
complete 13C-MFA and it is why the biomass composition is always used in
the practical implementation. 

* the experimental data that constrain the isotopomer balances. That is the
measured mass isotopologue / 13C enrichment pattern of intracellular
metabolic intermediates, Item 6, together with the measured extracellular
exchange fluxes which are normally expressed per unit biomass. The
measured labelling pattern is the 13C-MFA specific input which distinguishes
it from ordinary stoichiometric flux balance analysis.

Enzyme kinetics, the regulatory wiring of the network and the absolute
maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor are not used in the
steady-state isotopomer balance. Steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric
and isotopic constraint problem and is completely parameter-free with
respect to kinetics and regulation.

In the minimal formal sense the two independent experimental inputs are
therefore the stoichiometric network, 1, and the intracellular 13C labelling
patterns, 6. With the conventional closure of the network the biomass
reaction is written explicitly with the measured biomass composition, item
3, so that in practice the three items 1,3 and 6 are used and items 2,4 and
5 – maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks – are not
required for a steady state 13C-MFA. If biomass composition is regarded as
part of the definition of the stoichiometric biomass reaction, the two
distinct experimental requirements are stoichiometry and isotopic labelling.

I would say 3 of the listed items are needed for a steady-state 13C-MFA.

Stoichiometry is essential to write the mass balance equations and define the atom transitions for each reaction. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the fluxes via isotopomer balancing. Biomass composition is also required in practice because the biomass drain has to be explicitly defined in the network with a proper biomass reaction. The measured fractions of protein, lipid and carbohydrate set the carbon demand and the elemental formula of the biomass sink, so the system is closed and the flux distribution is uniquely identifiable. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used in the classical steady-state 13C-MFA formulation; steady state is an assumption on pools, not a kinetic or regulatory model.

In a strictly isotopomer based steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained
from the coupling of a stoichiometric network with the measured 13C
atom transition patterns.  

* Atom balances give for every reaction i

    v i S i = 0

with S the stoichiometric matrix of the network which is defined by 1.
Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. The network can be written without any
kinetic or regulatory information.

* The 13C information is introduced through the isotopomer balances

    v · f = 0

where f is the vector of fractional labelling, i.e. the measured
mass isotopomer or NMR multiplet distributions of the intracellular
metabolites, 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates.
The labeling data are the experimental constraints that make the
underdetermined stoichiometric system identifiable. Once the network and the
labeling data are known the steady state internal fluxes v can be obtained
by non-linear fitting of the simulated labeling to the measured labeling.

Enzyme kinetics 4. and the regulatory network 5. are not used in a
steady state flux balance / isotopomer balance formulation and the
maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor 2. is a scale up / process
parameter and plays no role in the flux calculation.

In practice a closed whole cell model is normally written with an explicit
biomass formation reaction. To write that reaction one needs the
elemental / macromolecular biomass composition 3. Biomass composition of
the organism, i.e. the protein/lipid/carbohydrate carbon demand which
together with the measured growth rate defines the biomass sink and closes
the carbon balance. With that closure the operational set of data that is
usually quoted for a 13C-MFA is 1 + 3 + 6, stoichiometry + a defined

mathematical requirement is the stoichiometric network and the measured
13C labeling, 1 and 6, i.e. two of the six listed items, with the biomass
composition being the conventional practical closure.

In a strictly isotopic sense steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric/isotope
mapping problem. Fluxes are obtained by fitting the network fluxes to the
measured isotopomer / mass isotopomer distributions under the steady state
constraints

dCi/dt = 0   and   dMi/dt = 0

where Ci is the concentration of metabolite i and Mi is its labelling
state. 

* Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with atom transitions is indispensable.
The network defines the mass balance constraints

S . v = 0

and the atom mapping that maps the labelling state of precursors onto
products, i.e. the labelling model Mi(v). Without a stoichiometric network
with defined atom transitions no isotopomer simulation can be made.

* Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is the experimental
data that the fluxes are fitted to. At isotopic steady state the measured
mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular, and usually also extracellular,
metabolites, e.g. MID from MS/NMR of a 13C tracer experiment, provide the
data vector which is matched to the simulation Mi(v). No kinetic
information is used in the fit.

That is the mathematical core of 13C-MFA. Enzyme kinetics and regulatory
networks are not required, and the maximum cell density of the organism in
a bioreactor is irrelevant for the isotopic fit. 

In practice the network is closed with an explicit biomass drain. The
biomass drain reaction is normally written from a measured or literature
biomass composition, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipids, carbohydrates
etc., together with a measured specific growth rate μ, so that the carbon
lost to biomass can be accounted for in the carbon balance and the
precursor fluxes to amino acids, nucleotides etc. can be expressed. With
that conventional closure the three routinely used inputs are

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry + atom mapping
3. Biomass composition to define the biomass reaction / carbon balance
6. Measured 13C labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates

Extracellular fluxes, including biomass formation rate, are also measured
in practice. If biomass is treated as a lumped, unlabelled sink the
biomass composition can be formally kept out of the isotopic fit and the
strictly indispensable inputs for the isotopic calculation are 1 and 6,
i.e. two of the six items listed, the stoichiometry and the labelling data.
Enzyme kinetics, regulatory networks and maximum cell density are not used
in steady state 13C-MFA.

The third essential piece in practice is a properly defined biomass sink. 13C-MFA at metabolic steady state is a stoichiometric / isotopomer problem, not a kinetic / regulatory one.

The flux solution is obtained from the stoichiometric network together with the
measured carbon atom transitions in the network. In practice that is

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. The network has to be written as a
set of mass balanced reactions so that the usual S . v =0 steady state
constraints and the atom mapping / isotopomer balances can be written down.
The biomass formation reaction is part of that stoichiometric description.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. The mass
isotopomer distributions, MIDs, measured by MS/NMR for intracellular
metabolites are the experimental constraints that resolve the otherwise
underdetermined flux degrees of freedom of the stoichiometric model.

In a closed, growth-coupled implementation the biomass sink has to be
defined. That is normally done with the measured biomass composition,
3. Biomass composition of the organism, i.e. the fraction of protein,
lipid, carbohydrate etc. which fixes the stoichiometric coefficients of
the biomass reaction. Once the biomass reaction is in the stoichiometric
model the composition is in fact already contained in 1.

The items which are not needed for steady state 13C-MFA are

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. Absolute
rates are normally expressed per gram dry weight or per cell, the maximum
attainable density is irrelevant for the flux ratios that 13C-MFA resolves.
The actual steady state growth rate / extracellular exchange rates are
needed, not the maximum cell density.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks. 13C-MFA is a
constraint-based, non-kinetic method. Kinetic parameters and regulatory
information are not used to obtain the steady state flux distribution.

In the minimal list from the six items the strictly essential information
is 1 and 6, i.e. stoichiometry + measured 13C labelling. This is normally
taught as the practical three item set 1,3,6 – stoichiometry, a defined
biomass composition/biomass reaction and the intracellular 13C labelling
patterns – with 2,4 and 5 being unnecessary for steady state 13C-MFA.

In a 13C steady state MFA the fluxes are obtained from the fit of a
stoichiometric / atom-mapping model to measured isotopomer data under
the assumption of metabolic and isotopic steady state.  That is
different from kinetic or regulatory modelling.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is indispensable.  The atom
transition matrix that defines how carbon atoms are mapped from
substrates to products in every reaction in the network is the
skeleton on which the isotopomer balancing equations are built.  In
practice the network is closed with a biomass drain reaction and the
biomass drain is written with the usual biomass composition, i.e.
fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., so that the carbon
demand for growth is accounted for in the stoichiometric model.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the
experimental data that the model is fitted to.  Measured mass
isotopomer distributions, e.g. MIDs from MS or NMR, for intracellular
intermediates together with the measured extracellular fluxes provide
the constraints that make the flux distribution identifiable.

These are the core MFA inputs.  The three items that are not needed
for a 13C steady state MFA are

* 2. Maximum cell density in a bioreactor.  Cell density is a process
parameter. MFA works with specific rates, i.e. per biomass or per
volume, at isotopic steady state, not with the attainable maximum
density.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics. Kinetic parameters are required for kinetic
flux modelling or for dynamic MFA, not for the stoichiometric/
isotopomer steady state formulation.
* 5. Regulatory networks.  Regulatory information is not used in the
stoichiometric isotopomer balancing.

Hence in the strict isotopomer fitting sense the indispensable
information from the list is the network stoichiometry and the
intracellular labelling data, items 1 and 6.  In routine practice the
stoichiometric model is made operational by writing a biomass
formation reaction with the organism specific biomass composition,
item 3, so that the network is mass balanced and the flux to biomass
can be quantified.  With that practical closure the three items
commonly quoted are 1, 3 and 6, whereas 2, 4 and 5 are not required
for steady state 13C MFA.

In a strictly stoichiometric 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained from
the atom balance equations

    S . v = 0
    M(v) = m_exp

together with the measured mass isotopomer distributions. 

* S is the stoichiometric matrix of the network that is used for the
atom-transition mappings. Without a defined stoichiometry and atom map
the relation between a flux distribution and the labelling that it
produces cannot be written down, so 1. metabolic reaction stoichiometry
is an absolute requirement.

* The labelling equations are closed by the experimental mass isotopomer
distributions of the intracellular intermediates that are measured by
MS/NMR. The 13C-MFA problem is the problem of finding a v which
reproduces the measured MIDs. Hence 6. the isotope labelling patterns
of metabolic intermediates is the second absolute requirement.

Enzyme kinetics 4., regulatory information 5. and the bioreactor
operational parameter maximum cell density 2. are not used in a
steady-state stoichiometric flux analysis. The flux calculation is
thermodynamic/ stoichiometric, not kinetic, and it is carried out at
metabolic steady state, dC/dt = 0, i.e. at constant pool sizes and
constant labelling, so that maximal growth / maximal cell density is
irrelevant.

In any closed implementation the network has to be closed to a biomass
sink. The biomass sink is normally written as a linear combination of
precursor metabolites whose stoichiometric coefficients are obtained from
the measured or literature biomass composition, i.e. the protein/lipid/
carbohydrate – and hence amino acid/nucleotide/fatty acid – demand of
the organism. In practice 3. biomass composition is therefore used to
define the biomass drain reaction that closes the carbon balance and
allows absolute flux normalisation.  If the biomass reaction is taken as
a given black-box sink the strictly mathematical requirements of the
13C labelling equations are 1 and 6, i.e. two of the six items listed,
stoichiometry + labelling.  This is the three-item experimental
implementation 1, 3 and 6 that is normally quoted in the literature, the
stoichiometry, the biomass composition needed for the biomass drain and
the measured 13C labelling patterns, with 2, 4 and 5 being unnecessary
for steady-state 13C-MFA.

3 items are required.

You also need the measured isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, 6, because those patterns are what constrain the flux split ratios via the isotopomer balances. In practice the biomass formation reaction has to be defined in the stoichiometric model, which requires the biomass composition, 3, i.e. the fractional protein, lipid and carbohydrate makeup, to close the carbon and redox balances at steady state. 

Maximum cell density, 2, is a bioprocess scale parameter and enzyme kinetics, 4, and regulatory networks, 5, are not used in the steady-state isotopomer balance formulation, so they are not required for the core 13C-MFA.

In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux vector v is obtained from the
steady state mass balances

    S . v = 0

together with the 13C labelling constraints.  In practice the
problem is

        min v   ||  xsim(v, S) – xmeas ||

subject to S v = 0 and v ≥ 0, where xsim is the labelling pattern
predicted from the network by the cumomer / isotopomer balances and
xmeas is the measured labelling.

Hence the two pieces of information that are mathematically
unavoidable are

* 1. The metabolic reaction stoichiometry S.  The stoichiometric
matrix is needed for the steady-state mass balance constraints and
for the propagation of 13C label through the network.  Without a
stoichiometric network there is no S v = 0 and no isotopomer
balance to solve.

* 6. The experimentally measured isotope labelling patterns of
metabolic intermediates, most conveniently the proteinogenic amino
acids or intracellular free metabolites derived from them.  The
labelling data are the constraints that make the flux split
uniquely identifiable.  In the limit S v = 0 alone 13C-MFA is
under-determined.

Maximum cell density in the bioreactor, enzyme kinetic parameters
and regulatory network topology are not used in the steady state
isotopomer balance formulation.  Steady state extracellular specific
rates, growth rate etc. are required experimentally but they are not
listed here.

In routine practice the biomass drain is written as a pseudo-reaction

    Biomass = Σ c i Pi

with c i the fractional composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate
etc.  The biomass composition 3 is therefore normally used to close
the stoichiometric network and to convert a measured growth rate into
a carbon drain from central metabolism.  With that operational
convention the model that is actually solved uses 1, 3 and 6, i.e.
stoichiometry + biomass definition + measured 13C labelling, while
2, 4 and 5 remain unnecessary for a steady state 13C-MFA.  The two
mathematically essential items are 1 and 6.
public_text.4:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are estimated from the
stoichiometric constraints of the network together with the constraints
that the measured isotopic distributions impose on the atom transitions.

* S v = 0   is the steady state mass balance.
The atom transition network, i.e. the metabolic reaction stoichiometry
in the sense of the carbon atom mappings, is therefore indispensable.
It is the stoichiometric matrix S, including the biomass drain reaction,
on which the flux variables are defined. Without a defined network the
isotopic constraints cannot be written down.

* The isotopic constraints themselves. The flux dependent steady state
isotopomer balances are

      v·E = 0

where E is the set of expected labelling patterns for the
intermediates. Those expected patterns are obtained from the measured
13C labelling of intracellular metabolites, or in practice of their
proteinogenic proxies, i.e. the measured isotope labelling patterns of
metabolic intermediates / amino acids. That is the experimental
information that makes the flux estimation uniquely solvable beyond
simple stoichiometric balancing.

That is the core of a 13C-MFA. Enzyme kinetics 4, regulatory networks 5
and the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor 2 are not used
in a stoichiometric, steady state 13C-MFA.

In practice the network is normally closed with a biomass formation
reaction. The stoichiometric coefficients of that drain reaction are
obtained from the measured biomass composition, i.e. the fractional
protein, lipid and carbohydrate content and the growth rate, which is
why the biomass composition 3 is routinely quoted as a third practical
input for a closed, carbon balanced 13C-MFA model. Strictly speaking the
core mathematical requirement is stoichiometry + labelling, i.e. items 1
and 6, two inputs, which becomes the commonly quoted three inputs 1,
3 and 6 when the biomass sink is written explicitly.
public_text.12:
In steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the mass and
isotopomer balance of the network

v . S = 0
and

M(v , x) = m meas

where S is the stoichiometric matrix of the network, v the vector of
unknown fluxes and m meas the measured mass isotopomer distributions of
the intracellular metabolites, generally obtained from proteinogenic
amino acids. The problem is therefore a stoichiometric + isotopomer
inverse problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Required. The stoichiometric
matrix S and the atom mapping that defines how carbon atoms are
transferred in each reaction are the basis of both the mass balance
v . S = 0 and of the isotopomer balance equations. Without a defined
network and an atom map no 13C fluxes can be calculated.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Required.
The measured 13C labeling of intracellular - or in practice
extracellular/proteinogenic - metabolites provides the experimental
constraints m meas that make the flux solution identifiable. In the
steady state formulation it is the 13C distribution that breaks the
flux balance degeneracy of S alone.

The remaining items are not part of a conventional steady state
13C-MFA.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. Not
required. Cell density / biomass concentration is a scale factor for
absolute rates. Steady state 13C-MFA works with specific rates,
e.g. mmol gDW-1 h-1, and with the measured specific uptake/secretion
and growth rates. A maximum achievable density is a bioprocess
limitation and is irrelevant for the isotopomer flux estimation.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. Not required. Kinetic constants, Vmax, Km,
etc., are needed for kinetic modelling and for dynamic MFA. Steady
state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric/inotopomer constrained optimisation/
fitting problem and is formally independent of enzyme kinetics and of
regulation.

* 5. Regulatory networks. Not required. Regulatory information is
not used in the isotopomer balance equations. Regulation may explain
why a flux is what it is, it does not enter the calculation of the flux
from stoichiometry and labelling.

* 3. Biomass composition. Not a strictly independent requirement for
the isotopomer calculation itself. The biomass formation can be entered
as a measured sink flux v biomass = µ, the specific growth rate, together
with the stoichiometric biomass drain reaction that is already part of
the network stoichiometry in item 1. In practice the biomass reaction
is formulated from the macromolecular composition - protein, lipid,
carbohydrate, etc. - so that item 3 is the practical way to build the
biomass stoichiometry that is contained in S. If the biomass reaction
is taken as given in the stoichiometric network, no separate
composition data are needed for the 13C flux solve, the core
information is items 1 and 6. If the formulation of the biomass reaction
is counted as a separate prerequisite the commonly quoted practical
set is stoichiometry + biomass composition + labelling data, i.e. items
1, 3 and 6.

In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are inferred from the way 13C is
distributed through a known chemical network. The inference is therefore
a purely stoichiometric / isotopomer balance problem and it is
kinetically and regulatory independent.

identifiability problem at isotopic steady state, enzyme kinetics and

parameter of the isotopic steady state flux problem. Specific

reaction. The stoichiometric coefficients of that reaction are obtained
from the elemental/ macromolecular composition of the biomass, i.e. the

model 1. If the biomass equation is taken as already contained in the

and the measured intracellular labelling pattern. With the conventional

required for the 13C-MFA per se.  This is usually quoted as the two

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round 0 discussion is highly convergent on what is essential for steady-state 13C-MFA versus what is not.

Core consensus:
* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is indispensable. The stoichiometric matrix S v = 0 and the carbon atom mappings define the isotopomer balances on which fluxes are fitted.
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are indispensable. Measured MIDs / NMR multiplets are the experimental constraints that make the underdetermined stoichiometric system identifiable. The isotopic steady state equations T(v)·M = 0 are closed by these data.

Items unanimously rejected:
* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – a process / scale-up parameter, not a flux constraint. Specific rates per gDW are used, not maximal attainable density.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics – not used in the stoichiometric/isotopomer formulation; Vmax/Km/regulation are for kinetic/dynamic MFA.
* 5. Regulatory networks – not used in the mass and carbon atom balances.

Disagreement / nuance on 3. Biomass composition:
* Strict isotopomer formalism: 1 + 6 are mathematically sufficient, with biomass treated as a given sink flux v_biomass = μ. Then biomass composition is formally part of the stoichiometric network definition.
* Practical laboratory implementation: the network is closed with an explicit biomass formation reaction. Its stoichiometric coefficients are obtained from the measured macromolecular composition – fraction protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc. – together with the growth rate. 2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree the core mathematical structure is stoichiometry + isotopomer balance, and that kinetics, regulation and maximum cell density are not part of a steady-state 13C-MFA. That is why 2,4 and 5 can be dropped.

Where I think the strict 1+6 reading misses the experimental reality is in what is meant by “Metabolic reaction stoichiometry” as listed in item 1. Item 1 gives the network topology and atom maps for central metabolism, but it does not give the stoichiometric coefficients of the biomass drain. To run a steady-state flux analysis the network has to be closed. The biomass formation reaction

Biomass = Σ c_i P_i

has to be written explicitly, and the c_i are not a generic stoichiometric constant. They are obtained from the measured macromolecular make-up of the cell, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipid and carbohydrate and the elemental formula of the biomass. That information is item 3, Biomass composition of the organism.

Without item 3 you cannot write the biomass sink in a chemically meaningful way and you cannot close the carbon and redox balance at steady state. The measured growth rate gives the flux through that sink, but the stoichiometry of the sink itself comes from the composition data. In practice you therefore need

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with atom mapping to set up S·v = 0 and the isotopomer transition equations,
3. Biomass composition to define the biomass reaction coefficients and close the network,
6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates, i.e. the measured MIDs, to constrain the flux split ratios via the isotopomer balances.

That is the operational three-item set that is routinely quoted as 1 + 3 + 6. If the biomass reaction is already taken as a given black-box part of S, the formal isotopomer fitting needs only 1 and 6, but for actually running the analysis the biomass composition is an independent required input from the list. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks remain unnecessary for the steady-state isotopomer calculation.

So from the six items listed the set that is actually required to run a steady-state 13C-MFA in practice is 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, 3. Biomass composition to define the biomass reaction and close the balance, and 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains highly convergent on what is essential and what is not, with the same split on biomass composition as before.

Core consensus held across rounds:
* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is indispensable. S·v=0 and the carbon atom mappings / atom transition network are the skeleton for mass and isotopomer balances. No 13C flux simulation can be written without an atom-mapped network.
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates is indispensable. Measured MIDs / NMR multiplets are the experimental constraints Msim(v)=Mmeas that make the under-determined S·v=0 identifiable. This is the 13C-specific data.
* Unanimously rejected: 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – a process/scale-up parameter, MFA uses specific rates per gDW at isotopic steady state; 4. Enzyme kinetics – not used in steady state stoichiometric/isotopomer fitting; 5. Regulatory networks – not part of mass/carbon atom balances.

Persistent disagreement / nuance on 3. Biomass composition:
* Strict isotopomer formalism view: once a biomass sink flux v_biomass = μ is taken as a given part of the stoichiometric model, the mathematics needs only 1 + 6. The biomass reaction then is formally contained in item 1. This is the “two-item core” repeatedly stated by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,16,17,18.
* Practical laboratory implementation view: to actually run a closed whole-cell steady state 13C-MFA the network must be closed with an explicit biomass formation pseudo-reaction Biomass = Σ c_i P_i. The coefficients c_i are not generic; they are set from the measured macromolecular composition – fraction protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc. – together with the measured specific growth rate. Without that definition carbon/redox balances are open, precursor fluxes to biomass are underdetermined and absolute flux scale cannot be fixed. Hence the operational set routinely quoted is 1 + 3 + 6. This is the “three-item practical” position argued most forcefully in round 1 by Colleagues 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,13,14 and reiterated here.

No new evidence in round 1 changes the earlier assessment. The discussion still oscillates between a formally minimal count of 2 items, 1 and 6, and the conventionally quoted operational count of 3 items, 1,3 and 6, with 2,4,5 unnecessary.

Unresolved for me: whether the question asks for the mathematically strict indispensable inputs from the list, i.e. two items, or for the operational inputs actually supplied to run a closed growth-coupled 13C-MFA in the lab, i.e. three items. Steady-state 13C-MFA is the stoichiometric / isotopomer inverse problem

S·v = 0 ,   Msim(v,S,atom map) = Mmeas

at metabolic and isotopic steady state, dC/dt = 0 , dM/dt = 0. It is a constraint based, non-kinetic problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with carbon atom mapping is indispensable. S and the atom transition maps define S·v = 0 and the function Msim(v) that propagates 13C from precursor to product. No isotopomer simulation can be written without a defined atom-mapped network.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is the experimental 13C constraint. The measured mass isotopomer distributions / NMR multiplets Mmeas of intracellular or proteinogenic metabolites are the data that make the otherwise under-determined S·v = 0 identifiable in the 13C sense. Regulatory networks do not enter the steady state isotopomer formulation. 13C-MFA works with specific rates per gDW per cell at isotopic steady state; Vmax, Km, regulation and a maximal attainable titre are process/kinetic parameters and do not enter S·v=0 or dM/dt=0.

3. Biomass composition to define the biomass drain and close C/redox balances
6. Measured 13C isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates

i.e. three of the six listed items, with 2 Maximum cell density, 4 Enzyme kinetics and 5 Regulatory networks unnecessary for steady-state 13C-MFA.
